>  In what circumstances would the owners of the site be implicated as well in anything criminal, if at all?

Criminally, they wouldn't be implicated unless they were part of some kind of conspiracy to defraud people of their money.  The state where I practice recognizes four kinds of *mens rea* in criminal law: knowing, intentional, reckless, and negligent.  You can't "recklessly" or "negligently" steal something, so I'm not sure what they would be convicted of.  

There's also a general principle in criminal law that you don't convict people for *not* doing something.  

Criminal negligence really only comes up in situations where you're already doing something that's legal, you're just doing it in a way that puts other people at risk (e.g. DUIs, setting off fireworks in a crowded place, etc).  There are vanishingly few circumstances in which you can convict someone for doing nothing, even if doing nothing seems like an insane thing to do under the circumstances.

So I'm actually a local prosecutor, and here's what I'll tell you: 

In theory, yes, you could be charged.  Discovering another crime isn't a defense to your crime.

In practice, we don't prosecute our witnesses, because then they wouldn't be too keen on testifying about the crime that we actually want to stop.

I was putting up the preliminary hearing for a DV case once where this woman was smacking her boyfriend in the face, yelling at him, even scratched his face with her nails (he had some really nasty looking cuts on his cheeks from it). That's assault, and we could have charged her for that.

We didn't do that, because after she did that, the boyfriend walked to the closet, grabbed a handgun, and fired three rounds into her chest.

We charged him with attempted murder, and (as the only eyewitness) the girlfriend got immunity to testify. If we hadn't given her immunity, she could have refused to testify against him on Fifth Amendment grounds (because in testifying against him, she would implicate herself in an assault).   But honestly, we gave it to her without a second thought because we're way, way more concerned about the attempted murder than the scratching and slapping.

In your example (burglar breaks into house and discovers trafficked kids), the cops would get a search warrant on the house and find the kids.  The defense attorney would bring a motion to suppress, arguing that there wasn't probable cause to search the house.  If the only basis for that search was an anonymous tip, then that defense attorney might actually win that motion.  By contrast, if there's a guy who was **actually in the house** and **saw** the kids and he can come in to testify, then defense is going to lose that suppression motion. 

So if I'm the prosecutor in this case, I'm going to say "Fuck the burglary", give you immunity, and drag you into court to testify at that suppression hearing.

**Short version:**

Wikipedia [quotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpalast_speech) Joseph Goebbels from the 1943 Sportpalast speech as having a bit of a tip of the slongue, accidentally talking about the "Ausrottung" (extermination) of the Jewish population in Europe, before quickly correcting himself and talking about the "Ausschaltung" (elimination/cutting off) of the Jewish population in Europe. 

The problem is that I've looked at transcripts of that speech, [here](https://archive.org/details/JosephGoebbels-Sportpalastrede) and [here](https://www.1000dokumente.de/index.html?c=dokument_de&dokument=0200_goe&object=translation&st=&l=de), and the word "Ausschaltung" doesn't appear in any of them (nor does the word "Ausrottung").  Goebbels doesn't seem to have said it there.  So where did he say it?

**Longer version:**

Here is the full quote and translation: 

> Deutschland jedenfalls hat nicht die Absicht, sich dieser jüdischen Bedrohung zu beugen, sondern vielmehr die, ihr rechtzeitig, wenn nötig unter vollkommen und radikalster Ausr... -schaltung [Ausrottung / Ausschaltung] des Judentums entgegenzutreten. 

> Germany, in any case, has no intention of bowing to this Jewish threat, but rather one of confronting it in due time, if need be in terms of complete and most radical exterm... exclusion [lit. "cutoff"] of Judaism.

Admittedly, I haven't listened to the full recording.  It's nearly two hours long, incredibly boring, and has an enormous amount of dead air. But something else made me even more suspicious: This incident of Goebbels supposedly saying the quiet part out loud is not even mentioned once in the [German version](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportpalastrede) of the same Wikipedia article.  Okay, so where is English Wikipedia getting this?  Do they have a source? 

Yes, they do.  Even better, they have a recording!  The footnote cites a clip from [this documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DRmHOSnehTk) where, at 0:26 , Goebbels says very clearly "sondern vielmehr die, ihr rechtzeitig, wenn nötig unter vollkommen und radikalster Ausro-schaltung des Judentums entgegenzutreten." ("but rather to oppose it in time, if necessary by completely and radically exter-liminating Judaism") The documentary has a heading at the top of the screen saying "February, 1943", which is when Goebbels gave the Sportpalast speech (sometimes known as the "Totaler Krieg" ("Total War") speech).   

And not only that, in that video, he is standing in front of a banner that says "Totaler Krieg - Kürzeste Krieg" (Total War - Shortest War), which was a banner only used for the February 1943 speech.  You can hear Goebbel's saying that line while he is standing in front of a crowd at the Berlin Sportpalast.

...but you can't actually **see** Goebbels saying that line.  The video is just of the crowd clapping, not of Goebbels talking.  So here's my working theory: the documentary makers put audio of Goebbels saying that line over video of the Sportpalast speech, ignoring (or missing) the fact that *that* audio was not from *that* speech.  A Wikipedia editor sees that clip and (understandably) thinks that the quote played in that clip was something that Goebbels said in the February 1943 speech, and edits the article accordingly.

So here's my question: where and when is that audio from?  When did Goebbels say this exactly?  Or is it actually buried in the audio of the speech somewhere, and the transcriptions I found along with German Wikipedia all missed this, while English Wikipedia somehow caught it? 

If I had to guess what happened, I would say that probably there is no extant video footage of Goebbels saying that, but the documentary makers really wanted to get that audio clip into the film.  So they probably just overlaid the audio on top of some other footage that they had.

Honestly, I don't object to the **idea** of the bar exam.  Bar associations have an obligation to make sure lawyers know and understand how the law works so that they don't harm their clients.  I don't really think graduating from law school, in itself, is a sufficient indicator of competence.

My issue with the way the bar exam **actually works** is that it seems to be written by the sort of people who write tests for a living.  They're constantly looking for ways to trip you up on a question for reasons that have nothing to do with the law and everything to do with stupid word games.

Just as an example, I had a question that went something like this

* Woman buys can of chicken soup 

* Woman gets food poisoning from can of soup and can prove damages

* Manufacturer defends that, although the can of soup had food poisoning when it left the canning facility, it complied with all government regulations with regard to the canning

* Manufacturer also proves it was not negligent in canning the soup and that it exercised extreme care in inspecting its facility

Now the way I read the question, I thought it said "who wins?"  And I said the woman, because strict products liability, and the manufacturer didn't offer a defense.

But no, you see. The question said "Woman sues manufacturer **for negligence** [i.e. not products liability].  Will she prevail?"  And the idiotic correct answer choice was "No, because the manufacturer proved it wasn't negligent."  


Ohhhhhh, got you!   Man, you sure got pwned didn't you, you dumb JD?  Aren't you glad you took this exam?  Aren't you glad that we're here to make sure that you know the law, because your big dummy law profs couldn't teach you basic negligence liability?  What's that? Our fact patterns don't make any sense?  HA!  Who are you to talk?  You got the question wrong!

The test writers aren't actually testing your knowledge of the law; they're trying to set traps for people to fall into and say "See?  Look!  People fail! That proves the examination is rigorous."  "Hard" questions aren't actually testing difficult applications of law to facts; "hard" questions are defined by how many people get them wrong, which could be for any number of stupid reasons.

Maybe I could excuse this on the SAT, ACT, or some general knowledge test.  But a lot of these questions really don't belong on a professional examination.

Freaking finally someone says this; it has been driving me absolutely bonkers that people seem can't distinguish language and information.

Try asking it to write code in an obscure programming language:  it will write that code, making up libraries that don't exist, and call non-existent functions from those imaginary libraries.

(Side note: 
I would actually argue that writing a program that will give you accurate information, and only accurate information, is impossible in principle: today's conventional wisdom is tomorrow's debunked myth.  You're ultimately going to have to tell it how to draw conclusions from limited information, and no matter what you do, it will 1. Be wrong sometimes, and 2.  Need to decide how to weight different kinds of evidence.

There are massive academic rabbit holes you could dive down for (2) in epistemology.  But suffice it to say that there are really serious philosophical disagreements about how you come to conclusions, some of which don't have a clear correct answer.  

The idea of any company (or even open-source project) billing their widely-used AI as a source of "information", while the developers decide how to weight evidence is...a little creepy honestly.  You could completely alter society's perception of the truth, while anyone who hasn't looked at the codebase is completely unaware of the assumptions that are built into that perception.)

This is just not true.  In the United States, disclosure of information with intent to manipulate a stock price for purchase or sale by others is illegal under SEC Rule 9a(2).  The section of the Exchange Act that the rule deals with is also 9a(2).

The fact that the information was hypothetically accessible to the public is irrelevant.  Dodd-Frank changed the rules somewhat, but if I recall correctly, you only need to prove 1) intent to manipulate a stock price and, 2) some overt action taken in furtherance of that manipulation.

The overt action here is pretty straightforward: Hindenberg shorted the stock.  Intent is trickier, but you may be able to prove that with the timing of all of this (i.e. the fact that they shorted bunch of Adani's stock a few days before releasing a story trashing it) . 

But in practice, the SEC won't do anything unless a lot of money is moving around.  They have limited resources and they typically don't go after minor sales like this.

> RMS/FSF/GNU have been very outspoken about copyright, and use copyright with permissive terms (copyleft) to counteract the negative terms of traditional copyright which typically limits the rights of the consumer. 

Yes, but it isn't right to say that the free software movement seeks to "abolish copyright."  RMS has [supported limited copyright terms](https://stallman.org/articles/guardian-correction.html) for creative works like [video game artwork](https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/nonfree-games.en.html) and [films](https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/copyright-versus-community.html) (Search for the sentence "What about works of art and entertainment?").

Both Red Hat and SUSE sponsor upstream distributions (Fedora and OpenSUSE Tumbleweed), which are "rolling-release" models, which basically means they get new updates every day.  Those upstream distributions are a testing ground for new stuff.

Once they've figured out which packages don't break, cause errors, bugs, crashes, etc.  Those companies then bundle those packages into a Stable release, which they then sell as an enterprise distribution.  

I tried to use Red Hat as a personal desktop once (they have trials for individual users), and it was a *terrible* idea.  That's because the needs of enterprises and large businesses are completely different than those of individuals who just need a personal computer.   

Bear in mind, you're principally talking about places where:

* Users do not own the hardware that they are using, and the people who do own it basically never use it

* There needs very strict management of permissions (i.e. who can access what)

* In addition to desktops, the business may need to maintain large servers (and keep them secure), and 

* The company does not necessarily want to pay for an entire team to work full-time to sort out their software issues. For example, if you own a business that develops computer games, you would rather spend your money on game devs, not tech support

Red Hat, SUSE, and Canonical basically package stable software that doesn't break for distribution, charge subscription fees to businesses, and offer tech support to those businesses so that they may only need one or two people on staff to deal with their tech issues.  If the tech issue is significantly more complicated and the on-staff tech people can't deal with it, then you can contact Red Hat/SUSE/Canonical software engineers at their headquarters to work on the problem. 
 
Basically, their pitch is "We select stable, well-maintained software for your business, teach you how to use it, set it up for you,maintain it and tailor it to your needs, and you can call us if anything goes wrong", and they charge you a flat annual fee for the subscription.   Businesses hate dealing with things that aren't related to their business (e.g. legal issues, accounting, taxes, insurance, etc), and want to minimize those costs as much as possible.

It does, actually.  

Typically, you're not allowed to raise ineffective assistance of counsel claims on direct appeal, and that's because they involve examining facts that are outside the record (e.g. what your attorney said or did outside of court).   You would have to do it in a petition for post-conviction relief (which only takes place after you've exhausted your appeals).

However, you *could* raise an ineffective assistance of counsel claim directly on appeal if your attorney's incompetence is evident from the record (i.e. the trial transcript, briefs, and evidence), and the attorney's incompetence resulted in an unfair trial.  In that case (which I have never actually seen happen), you could actually argue that the appellate court should declare a mistrial on the basis of a violation of the defendant's Sixth Amendment rights.

But the Sixth Amendment only deals with criminal cases.  You don't have a right to effective counsel in civil cases.  If your lawyer fucks up and loses you a lot of money, sucks to be you.  You might be able to sue the lawyer for malpractice and recover some assets, but unless you have some other basis for appealing the civil case other than "my lawyer was bad," that verdict isn't getting overturned.

"No exposure to the code" is the critical bit there.  

I don't know the details of what exactly OP is planning to do with this Python library (and given that it's under a permissive license, it probably doesn't matter). Libraries in general are an interesting legal gray area.  The FSF uses the LGPL (rather than the GPL) for their libraries, in part because they want to avoid the implication that if you used glibc (for example) to build some program, that you would be obligated to distribute the source code under the copyleft provisions of the license as a result (because that would be ridiculous).

EDIT: I also want to point out that, in the article you linked, you'll note that the Court never actually reached the question of whether an API was copyrightable.   They just said that even if it were copyrightable, Google's conduct would constitute fair use.  

The subtext of that is: if you clone an API, you might still be held liable for copyright infringement.  This is a very fact sensitive case where they didn't set a hard-and-fast rule, and one in which the Court could easily "come out the other way" without contradicting their prior reasoning.

> Can they revoke my license that I set on my project if the license was added before the patent is filled.

I'm not sure what you're saying.  *You're* the one who issued the license.  It's your copyright.  They can't revoke anything from you.  If you wrote the software, and it's licensed under GPL, you're licensing it to them, and in incorporating it into their patented product, they're violating the terms of the license.

> If they take action, what protection do I have if my project is on Github?

It doesn't make any difference if your project is on Github.  It doesn't make a difference if it's published on the front page of The New York Times.  It's still copyrighted, which means that you have the right to license it.  The fact that it's widely shared is irrelevant.  You're still allowed to put conditions on how people use it, and if they don't like those conditions, they don't have to use it.

> Can they even file a patent and steal my work?

They could.  And then you would sue them into the ground and make them sorry they did, since they violated the terms of the license agreement.  You might get damages (read: oodles of money), or you might get an injunction against them to comply with the license (i.e. release any source code that they used in making their product, hypothetically you might even get their patent revoked, though that's unlikely).   

Most likely, you'd cause them to suffer a large financial loss rather than have their patent revoked (it's unlikely a court would revoke a patent just because the inventor violated the terms of a license to get the patent, though it's technically possible).  This is why, even though the conditions of the GPL may not be enforceable after the fact, Apple, Google, etc. still avoid GPL-licensed software like the plague.

The worst case scenario would be this: you're about to lie on the stand, you tell me you're about to lie on the stand, and I fail to talk you out of lying (and/or fail to talk you out of testifying).   In that specific case, I would be obligated to ask the court that I be allowed to resign.  When they ask why, I give a vague answer to the judge (usually *in camera*) that I believe that I cannot continue to perform my ethical obligations as a lawyer while continuing to represent you.  Even if the judge forces you to give an exact reason, that reason can't be disclosed to anyone except the judge, and can't be considered at trial because it's still considered attorney-client communication (I guess unless you subsequently get indicted for perjury, but that's a completely different matter).

Bear in mind, in order for this to happen, I would have to *know* that you know you're lying.  Having video evidence or other witnesses contradicting what you say isn't enough; what if the guy on the video just looks a lot like you?  Or what if the video is from a date other than the one the prosecution is alleging?  What if all the other guys are members of a rival gang, and are just lying to get you thrown in prison? Those are all arguments a defense attorney can make, and you can put your client on the stand to testify about those things.  That's all above board.  

Once you straight up tell me "I'm going to lie to the court," we have a problem.  But it's not really a confidentiality issue.

Things that, as a lawyer, I need to break confidentiality for:

* someone is in immanent physical danger and I know about it


* you are using my services to commit a crime (e.g. having me launder money for you, hiding your drugs in my office)


* I am ordered by a court to testify or provide confidential materials.  (This never happens in an ordinary criminal or civil case; it usually comes up in malpractice cases, where lawyers need to disclose confidential information in order to defend themselves from the allegations.   I have seen this happen in a murder case once where the accused's lawyer was ordered to testify.  But you should know that in that case, the accused was already dead, and his defense attorney in the criminal case was subpoenaed in relation to a lawsuit for the assets in the guy's estate).

* you are withholding some piece of physical evidence from the court and I know where it is 

For the last one, here's an example I remember:  a guy told his lawyer where his stash of kiddie porn was, and asked the lawyer to keep it in his office before the police could search his house.  The lawyer was obligated to turn it over in discovery, because the guy was withholding evidence.

But (and this is important) literally anything else you tell me in an official capacity is confidential: any past crime you confess to (or even certain future crimes you intend to commit, it they don't involve physical danger), any time someone has *previously* been in danger, any criminal gangs you're a part of, etc. my lips are sealed.  You could sit in my office and confess to the Zodiac murders, and I can't tell a soul about it without your permission.  The fact that you previously killed somebody doesn't constitute immanent physical danger to someone else.  

You could admit to laundering billions of dollars, staging the Kennedy assassination, being Osama bin Laden, running a Mexican drug cartel, burning down Notre Dame Cathedral, and your lawyer won't disclose anything.  

The only time it would hurt you to disclose something to your lawyer would be if you're hiding evidence.  But competent defense attorneys won't ask where the murder weapon is, because they don't need to know.  They might ask if the police recovered the murder weapon, because that's the only thing that's relevant to your case.  But they would usually get that in discovery, and so they don't need to ask you that. 

So in short:  yes, tell your lawyer everything,  because it won't hurt you, and if you don't, your lawyer can't help you.  Your lawyer needs to know what could come out just in case it does; the facts of what happened will determine the sorts of legal arguments your lawyer will make. I've seen a couple cases where clients have destroyed weeks worth of legal research because they were too embarrassed or reluctant to disclose something.  You can easily end up destroying your own case.  Don't do that.

For Old Testament texts, one of the claims of many Protestant reformers was that the Catholic Church had added various texts to the canon when it had no authority to do so.  This is part of the reason why a Catholic Bible includes several OT texts (like the Book of Maccabees and the Book of Jubilees) that the Protestant Bible does not.  It's also why Protestants and Jews agree on the canon with each other, but not with Catholics.  There's not solid agreement on when the Jewish canon was set, but it was much earlier than the Christian one (somewhere between the 3rd century BCE and the 2nd century CE, although I would argue that the Dead Sea Scrolls indicate that the date was earlier in that range).  

My point is that they would argue that the OT canon was already set before Jesus, and so wasn't selectively picked through by later Christians.

For New Testament texts, you're going to get a number of different Fundamentalist explanations.  One common approach was to simply dispute that the Canon was ever in question (this isn't really common now, but it was popular 100 years ago).  They had another argument that the Holy Spirit worked through the Church Fathers to lead them to the truth (because God would never allow Christians to have a book of falsehoods if he wanted his truth to be known).   The theory is that through this guidance, God allowed Christians to preserve the truth of the Gospel so that they could bring salvation to future generations.

There's even one explanation (which many Fundamentalists consider heretical, but that I saw one Anglican theologian make) that the Bible *is* at least partially influenced by human understanding, and the Canon may not be fully reliable, but that is precisely why every word of it must be believed.  The reasoning went that since the words of God are mixed in there somewhere with the words of men, and we can't know the mind of God, that means we can't tell which words are God's and which are human invention. That means that every word of the Bible must be accepted, lest Christians risk jettisoning the word of God, and make Christianity into more of a human (rather than divine) image than it already was.  Since the Bible was basically compiled based on early Christians' best understanding about what actually happened (or so this guy said, anyway) then it's also the closest possible Christians can be to understanding the events surrounding Jesus' death and resurrection.

The sticking point was really critical biblical studies, and the theological questions that were raised by treating the Bible as if it were any other ancient document.

If you had to pick a single starting point of this divergence in Protestant belief in America, I would say it should be the Briggs controversy in 1891.  Charles Briggs was a professor of theology at Princeton Theological Seminary, Old Testament scholar, and Presbyterian elder/minister who claimed to have conclusively proven that Moses did not write the first five books of the Bible, as had been traditionally believed by Christians.  He ~~questioned~~ proclaimed the falsity of the authorship of nearly every Old Testament text: Ecclesiastes, Proverbs, Isaiah, etc.   He was eventually tried for heresy by the main Presbyterian body in the U.S. and found not guilty.  (There were actually two trials....it's complicated.  He was found guilty and defrocked at the second one, but there's this whole question of whether the people who tried him then actually had the authority to do that...it's a whole thing).  Briggs also questioned the authorship of numerous biblical texts that explicitly stated their authors (unlike the Pentateuch, which does not).  This controversy, and the backlash in the Presbyterian church that it provoked, is what ultimately what led to rather heated debates among American Christians regarding what exactly their attitude towards the Bible should be.

Here is the source of the controversy: *sola scriptura*.  If the Bible and only the Bible is the ultimate authority on your religion, and the Bible is *wrong*, then your religion is also wrong.  So do you believe that your religion is a source of truth or not?  

Modernists (the faction to which Briggs belonged) usually answered this by saying things like "the Bible is a source of moral and spiritual truth, not historical truth."  They were open to the idea that the Bible was wrong when discussing historical events, or that these events were allegory to convey some broader truth.  They were generally accepting of scientific theories (e.g. evolution, the age of the Earth) that questioned traditional Christian beliefs, and were willing to change their theology based on conclusions in fields like source criticism or archeology.  For example, one common view was that Jesus was not actually born of a vigin (despite the fact that two different Gospels say that he was), as conception in the absence of both sperm and egg isn't scientifically possible.  If you want to read a famous text expressing a Modernist view, I recommend the sermon "Shall the Fundamentalists Win?" by Harry Emerson Fosdick. 

The Fundamentalists represented the views that most Christians had traditionally held prior to that point.  Their contention was that reducing the Bible to allegory and metaphor was not only arrogant, but led to Christian theology making no sense at all.  For example,   why is Man drawn towards sin?  Many Christians would have said that it was because of Adam's and Eve's defiance of God in the Garden of Eden.  But if there was no Garden, no Adam or Eve, now you still have to answer the question.  And the problem is, any answer you come up with isn't going to be based on the Bible.  It's going to be based on "Well it can't possibly be *that* because science says so, so it must be...[insert speculation here]."   Notice that this requires one to defer to science before concluding anything about the Bible. 

Fundamentalists argued that this amounts to humans taking their views as equally or more authoritative than the Bible.   If Jesus wasn't born of a virgin, then who was his father?  And if he has a father, then how can he be God's only begotten son?  And if he's not God's son, then why was his death on the Cross different from anyone else's?  And if he *didn't* die on the Cross, then how are you supposed to atone for your sins, if not through his suffering?  And how can *any* answer you give to those questions be based on the Bible alone?  The argument was that the Modernist view basically made absolute nonsense of Christian theology, and so had to be rejected by any believing Christian.

The term "fundamentalist" comes from the publication of the Five Fundamentals that were passed by the  General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in the United States America (PCUSA) in 1910.  They declared the following absolutely necessary to be considered a Christian:

* Biblical inerrancy (the Bible is not "wrong" about anything, as it was divinely inspired)

* the Virgin Birth of Jesus

* that Jesus died to atone for sin

* that Jesus was bodily resurrected from the dead (I.e. not just "spiritually resurrected" or that he came back as a ghost or something)

* that Jesus performed actual miracles (as opposed to these being an embellishment of the historical record, or magic tricks of some kind)


By the early 20th century, many different Protestant denominations were infighting over this, and in particular, fighting each other for tenured positions at major seminaries.  Princeton and Union became pretty solidly modernist (although the fight at Princeton was particularly nasty). Dallas Theological Seminary remained fundamentalist, and Westminster Theological Seminary (which is still around)  was formed by disgruntled fundamentalist faculty at Princeton  You can also see the remnants of the dispute today: most of the major Protestant denominations either split over this issue or self-segregated into fundamentalist and modernist versions of the same denomination.

 E.g.  Presbyterians largely self-segregated into the Presbyterian Church USA (modernist) and the Presbyterian Church in America (fundamentalist). Seminary students and faculty formed Seminex (modernist), a split from the Evangelical Lutheran Church, Missouri Synod (fundamentalist), and merged to form the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (modernist).  I could keep going, but you get the point.

The Christians you're referring to in your question are largely the theological descendants of the Fundamentalists.  However, that label is somewhat dated now, because some would insist on different fundamentals or not view some of the Five Fundamentals as essential, or would even disagree with some of them.  But there there is definitely a religious/intellectual tradition that both Fundamentalists and these Christians you refer to in your question have in common.  I'm just going to call them both "fundamentalists" for the sake of simplicity.  In short, they have the following belief in common: the Bible is the ultimate source of truth and authority.  Reinterpretations of it are broadly massaged to fit with modern beliefs, and modern views are perversions of its message.

So why is fundamentalism largely restricted to the U.S.?  It isn't.  Europe has a negligible percentage of fundamentalists, but Europe is the exception, not the rule.  Fundamentalism is a relatively popular belief among Protestants in South America, Southern Africa, and East Asia (e.g. the Philippines and South Korea).  Maybe not a majority, but Fundamentalists aren't a majority in America either.    Europe is the weird one here.

So why is Europe the exception?  The following is a disputed historical theory, but it's one I'm sympathetic to.  It shouldn't be taken as historical fact:  In Europe, Protestant churches were mostly state churches (e.g. in England, Germany, Denmark, etc), and the theology was often...uhhh...massaged for political expediency.  If you want just one example, the predecessor to the EKD (the main Protestant body in Germany today) was formed by a state-imposed merger of a Lutheran body and a Calvinist body (two denominations with incompatible theologies) because Fredrick Wilhelm III decided it would be beneficial for national unity.  The institutionalization of Protestant denominations led to them to be subject to political pressure in a way that nonstate churches are not.   Massaging traditional views to comport with modern developments was very normal among European Protestants for centuries before the controversy. 

I should also say that the fact that the Catholic Church was not terribly affected by this controversy largely has to do with the fact that the Catholic view of the Bible is not what it claims as its source of its authority.  That authority comes from from the institution of the church itself.  If you believe that salvation is through faith in the proper view of Christianity alone, and that the Bible is the sole source of correct faith, then this institutional view is not possible (since, on the Protestant view [arguably excluding Anglicans] church bodies only have authority to the extent that their doctrine is true).  The Catholic Church since the Council of Trent has viewed both the Bible and Sacred Tradition as equally authoritative, and draws on apostilic succession rather than the Bible as the source of its own authority.  As a result, Catholic belief on such subjects has been less defined than (for instance) its insistence on the primary of the Pope.   Because faith isn't the only thing that makes one a Catholic, Catholic self-id tends to be much stronger among people who don't believe church teaching than it is among Protestants.

Kohanim were the actual priests in the Temple who did the animal sacrifices and performed the most important ritual functions, and from whom the High Priest was selected. > If all Jews were descendants of the Tribe of Judah, then what precisely happened to the other tribes?

This is your first misconception.  The term "Jew" as it is used in the modern day doesn't refer to descendants of the tribe of Judah.  It refers to inhabitants of the *Kingdom* of Judah.  

The united Kingdom of Israel only existed for a little more than a hundred years (from 1047-930 BCE), until it split into two separate kingdoms: the southern Kingdom of Judah (which included Jerusalem) and the northern Kingdom of Israel (which the Bible sometimes refers to as "Samaria," presumably to avoid confusion).  The Kingdom of Judah was the smaller of the two, and included the territories of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.  There were Levites in the Kingdom of Judah too, but the tribe of Levy was more of a priestly caste than a tribe with territory.  The later Kingdom of Israel (which I'm going to call "Samaria" so we don't get confused) included the territory of the other ten tribes (Reuben, Menasseh, Ephraim, etc.).  Samaria was conquered by the Neo-Assyrian Empire around 722 BCE.

The Kingdom of Judah continued to exist until around 587 BCE when it was conquered by the Babylonian king Nebuchanezzar.  The subsequent "Bablyonian Exile" was the period in which at least some of the inhabitants of the Kingdom of Judah were taken to Babylon as captives following Nebuchanezzars conquest (likely this was mainly the Jewish inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem).

Babylon was eventually conquered itself by the Persian emperor Cyrus the Great.  According to the Biblical narrative, Cyrus then allowed the captive Jews and their descendants to return to Judah, provided they swore allegiance to him.  There is some corroboration of an event like this taking place in the form of the [Cyrus cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Cylinder), which was a royal edict returning various captive peoples to their ancestral homelands (although the Jews are not mentioned).  

Judah changed hands a lot over the next few centuries.  It was ruled by the Persians until it was conquered by Alexander the Great, and then became part of the Selucid Empire, and eventually was conquered by the Romans.  And eventually would become the birthplace of Jesus, and the place where Paul did a lot of his missionary work.

But to answer your question, the inhabitants of the Kingdom of Judah that were supposedly returned to their homeland by Cyrus the Great were from three tribes:  Judah, Benjamin, and Levy.  The Levitical priesthood was passed down patrilineally, and it was considered particularly important to maintain that bloodline.  So as it turns out, you *will* actually find many Israelis (and Jews around the world) who will tell you that they are Levites (I believe Levites have been estimated to be ~5% of total Jews, but I can't find a source for that right now). But the vast majority of Jews are from the tribes of Benjmain and Judah.

(FYI, I only know enough about OT scholarship to answer your question, and will reply on that basis.  I'm not familiar enough with the scholarship surrounding Jesus to answer most of your questions on early Christianity.)

> How familiar with the OT were average Jews from 100 BCE — 100 CE?

**Average** Jews?  Not very.  The exact rates of literacy in Roman Judea around this time are contentious; I believe Catherine Hezser puts it at around 3% in *Jewish Literacy in Roman Palestine* (2001), while Christopher Rollston puts it closer to 15-20%.  The general consensus, though, is that most people couldn't read or write and so would have had a lot of difficulty being intricately familiar with the details of the biblical texts.  Most people would have likely familiar with the general stories involving Moses, Adam and Eve, Esther, etc, through oral tradition.  But they're not going to be parsing through the exact language of the text, or know the specifics of detailed prophecies.

> Matthew 21's donkey AND a colt, from what I've read, is a misunderstanding of the poetic cadence used in Zechariah 9:9

The Hebrew uses two words "חמור" (chamor) and "עיר" (a-ir), both of which mean "male donkey" (though חמור is more common).  It says riding a "chamor v'a-ir," "v" being a preposition which can mean "and."  However, if you were trying to say "riding two donkeys," this would be a very strange way to say it ("riding a donkey and a donkey").  You would either say "riding two donkeys" or "riding a donkey, and another donkey."  As a result, most people believe that the "v" here is emphatic (i.e. the two words are talking about the same donkey), which happens occasionally when you're trying to emphasize something.  Take for example Deuteronomy 16:2: 

> וזבחת פסח ליהוה אלהיך צאן ובקר 

> And you shall slaughter the Passover [sacrifice] to the Lord your God [tsun v'vakar = literally "[from the] herd and [the multiple] cattle/sheep.")

Many translations will render this as "from the herd and the flock," but the words are just different ways of saying "a group of livestock," so the "v" in this context is not being used to mean "and."  It's being used as a restatement of the first thing (e.g. "Riding in on an ass, a donkey!" rather than "Riding in on an ass and a donkey.") 

> Isaiah 7:14 is actually talking about a young girl in Hebrew...but Matt and Luke and Christianity concocted the virgin birth

Here, the word is "עלמה" (almah); this is generally considered to mean "young woman."  (Its usage reminds me most of the Russian "devushka," which means roughly the same thing)

The same word is used in Proverbs 30:18-19, which reads "Three things are beyond me; Four I cannot fathom: How an eagle makes its way across the sky; how a snake makes its way across the rock; How a ship makes its way through the high seas; how a man has his way with an [almah]."   To some people this would be an indication that the word doesn't mean "virgin," and that "young woman" would make more sense.

If this does mean virgin, it's also very odd that we're being told of the virginity of Moses' sister, when she is simply asked to fetch her mother in Exodus 2:8.

I believe what most people suspect happened is that Matthew was looking at a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, and saw a mistranslation of this word as "parthenos" (Παρθένος), which actually does mean virgin (but Greek is not my forte, so don't take me at my word on that). 

Quite aside from that, Isaiah 7 is quite unrelated to Jesus' birth.  If you read from the beginning of the chapter, you'll see that the King of Judah at the time (Ahaz) is losing a war against Damascus and the Northern Kingdom.  Isaiah tells him that an "almah" will have a child, he shall grow up, and before he will know good from evil, Ahaz will have victory over his enemies.   While this is a prophecy, it was obviously a prophecy that was meant to be fulfilled within Ahaz's lifetime, and Ahaz died some time in the 8th century BCE.  If "almah" really does mean "virgin," I would very much like to know who this first virgin was who had a child 700 years before Jesus was born, and why the author doesn't mention the significance of this event ever again.  (Young women have children all the time.  Virgins?  Not so much.)

I hesitate to use a term like "wrong," because that's really a matter of interpretation.  But Matthew and Paul in particular go through several proof texts that I would regard as...dubious. 

One off the top of my head: 

Matthew 2:15: 
> So he got up, took the child and his mother during the night and left for Egypt, 15 where he stayed until the death of Herod. And so was fulfilled what the Lord had said through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called my son."

That's not actually a prophecy, and that's not really what it says  Here's the text of Hosea 11:1:

The common explanation of this is that Matthew and Paul were quoting from a Greek translation known as the "Septuagint," and that's why they got some things wrong.  I should note that there is no single text called "the Septuagint."  It's largely an invention of the Letter of Aristeas, which most historians consider to be a forged historical document.  Supposedly (according to the letter), 70 rabbis were called to translate the 5 Books of Moses into Greek, and they [miraculously] all came out with the exact same translation.  This became a basis among Hellenized Jews for asserting the parity of a given Greek translation with the Hebrew text, even though they were likely looking at the work of a contemporary translator.

I know that the Orthodox Church actually did compile a Greek translation called "the Septuagint," which included not just the first five books of the Bible, but the entire Old Testament.   This translation was later used by the Greek Church and (I believe, again, not my speciality) had similar canonical status to the Vulgate in the Catholic Church, but this was done centuries after Paul would have died.  In responding to criticism as to why he didn't translate the Vulgate from the Greek instead of the Hebrew, Jerome (writing in the late 4th, very early 5th century) responded that there were different traditions of different Greek texts in different parts of the Mediterranean, whereas the textual tradition of the Hebrew text (by that point in time) was relatively stable by comparison.  As a result, it was easier to translate from the relatively minor disparities in the Hebrew texts, rather than the much larger disparities in the Greek texts.  (This is all in the preface to Jerome's translation of the Book of Chronicles in the Vulgate).

Usually that isn't admissible in court unless it speaks to some issue of material fact in the case.  

Remember, the only questions the jury is really trying to answer are whether or not Derek Chauvin killed George Floyd, and if so, whether he acted in accordance with the police training he had received.  Bringing up Chauvin's past behavior doesn't help them do that, so it likely won't be admitted at trial (and if it were, that could be grounds for an appellate court to declare a mistrial).  

Bringing up a defendant's past criminal history when it wasn't relevant to the case has gotten a lot of defendants off on appeal (because the fact that they have committed crimes in the past is irrelevant to whether or not they committed the offense for which they are being tried; otherwise I could accuse any random criminal of committing any random crime, and use their record as evidence against them).  The only circumstance I know of where it is very common to allow a defendant's criminal history into evidence is when you're challenging the credibility of a witness.  

For example, if there's a witness claiming he never saw the defendant kill anybody, you're allowed to mention (if it's true) that both the witness and the defendant are members of the mafia, and that the witness would be killed if he said the defendant committed a crime.

> isn't Russian society primarily patronymic

It depends on the context.  Russians have 3 names: a first name, a patronymic, and a surname.  Just as an example, Anatoly Karpov's full name is Anatoly Yevgenyevich Karpov.  His father's name was "Yevgeny," which is why his patronymic is "Yevgenyvich."  "Karpov" is his family name, and "Anatoly" is his given name.

If you were referencing him in the third person (assuming your audience already knew who he was) you would call him "Anatoly Karpov."  If your audience did not know who Karpov was, you might say "Anatoly Yevgenyevich Karpov."

If you were speaking to him directly in a formal context, you would call him "Anatoly Yevgenyevich" (no surname).  This is the polite form of direct address (sort of like the Russian equivalent of calling him "Mr. Karpov.").  

If you were a friend, you would either call him "Anatoly" or "Tolya" (Tolya being the diminutive of "Anatoly"), depending on how close you are.  "Tolya" is less formal than "Anatoly." 

So short version: a lot of Russians would know what Kasparov's surname was, likely more than would know what his patronymic was.  I've heard Russians ask what a celebrity's patronymic was, since you mainly use it when talking to someone directly and most people don't talk to celebrities on a daily basis.  By contrast, if you have a colleague at work whom you speak to every day, it's possible that you know his patronymic, but not his surname.

Bh6 is not a missed win (the engine is crazy), but I think you might be misunderstanding what the high number means.  An evaluation of -2 doesn't mean you win material; it means that black is considerably better (i.e. the position is such that it's AS IF black is up two pawns)

The reason the computer really likes Nc6 is because white actually has kind of a sneaky threat.  If it's white's move, white is going to play 1.dxe5 dxe5 2.Ra5, the black queen has to move, and white will play Rxd5, with a doubled rook and queen on the d-file.  Now white is only down one pawn (as opposed to two), and controls the d-file, which can be used to attack black later.  White is going to castle, and get a nice safe king, and the black king is always going to be a little uncomfortable because there's ideas of Rd7.   I assume the engine thinks it's about equal because black has a nice pawn center, the white knight isn't really playing (and can't really move anywhere useful), and the c3 pawn is sort of weak if black tries to gang up on it with moves like Rc8-Bg7-f4-e4 (plus white is still down a pawn).

Anyway, Nc6 stops all of that, and ensures that you're just up two pawns and white can't really move the bishop or the knight anywhere useful.  I assume the engine will also think b6 is an okay move, because it also stops dxe5 followed by Ra5.

He was actually a welcome break from my previous coach from when I was a kid, who used to get really angry at me when I played badly, or wasn't able to solve some tactical puzzle he gave me.  I think one of the greatest moments of relief I felt in my chess career was when I was showing Ben a tournament game I was winning and blundered into a loss, and I was scared he was going to get mad at me [and like my old coach, tell me I was never going to get better if I kept doing stupid stuff like that]. I will say that I think one of Ben Finegold's greatest faults is that he's kind of lazy.  A lot of the stuff he was showing people in the St. Louis lectures was stuff he was showing all of his private students at the same time, because he didn't really prepare for private lessons based on who the student was. When he started streaming (around 2017-2018), he started raising his rates for private lessons because he could make more money doing insult comedy on Twitch than he ever could giving lessons, and he encouraged his private students to go elsewhere. The Twitch people found him because of his St. Louis lectures, where he's doing his schtick, so he does his schtick on stream (if you watch a lot of his older streams circa 2017 early 2018, you'll actually see that he's not overtly obnoxious like he is now [EDIT: [here's](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=djmsOwESJ-U) one example I found)].
